utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Brdjanin, do I take it that you can follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Interpretation good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone was not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, together with Ann Sutherland, assisted, as ever, by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome back, and thank you. Appearances for the Defence? One moment, Mr. Ackerman. I don't think we can proceed with this stack of files obstructing the view. I know that this is not an easy courtroom to work in but I obviously need -- it's not just Mr. Ackerman, it's the whole Defence bench that I need to have in view, all the time. Now I can't see Mr. Cunningham. That's better. Okay. So appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. In case you've forgotten, my name is John Ackerman. I'm lead counsel for Mr. Brdjanin. I'm here this morning with our new co-counsel David Cunningham and Barbara Baruch and with Vesna Anic who is serving as our interpreter in the absence of Ms. Jevtovic who is hospitalised and we hope will be with us soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think even she is hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, this case is medically challenged, Your Honour, if you haven't noticed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Welcome back, Mr. Ackerman. Thank you and on behalf of my two colleagues, Judges Janu and Taya, apart from welcoming both of you back, we are happy that you are fully recovered and that we look forward to resuming and proceeding with this case, hoping that we won't have a repetition of what took place the last two months but most important thing is that you're back in good shape, both of you. So I understand there are a few things that you need to raise and we also have several issues to clear up before we can proceed. In the meantime, I also welcome you on behalf of the Trial Chamber, Mr. Cunningham and look forward to working with you. The description that we've had from Mr. Ackerman as well as from the office about your qualifications is very encouraging so we really do indeed look forward. Thank you. So shall we start with you, Madam Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only application that I have relates to the witness and I wonder if we could go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (Redacted) (Redacted) 2 (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We also sent to the Registry for filing yesterday our response to the 92 bis motion regarding Bosanski Petrovac, and that will also be filed this morning and delivered to Your Honours I suppose sometime today. I will ask permission to leave as soon as we finish these preliminaries. I am not supposed to actually be here until the 1st of June. My doctor told me not to do this, but I wanted to come this morning just to deal with any of these preliminary matters that may need to be taken care of, Your Honour. The one thing I wanted to make a matter of record is this: For the two months that we have not been here, I have been unable to have a confidential communication with my client because the Registry denied my requests for him to have confidential telephone contact with either Ms. Jevtovic or Mr. Peric or Mr. Bojic, our two investigators, and our legal assistants, and therefore there was no way for me to communicate with him. I know the Trial Chamber was aware of that denial because they sent a copy of the letter to you. So it has made it very -- extremely difficult for us to make any progress regarding the preparation of the case for the Defence and the direction and assistance to our investigators in the field in Banja Luka. I don't understand that rule. That has never Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. been the rule until I made this request. Throughout the entire Pre-Trial of this case, Mr. Brdjanin was able to have those kind of communications with Ms. Maglov, who was not co-counsel at that point, and Your Honour, I just want it on the record that I complained bitterly about it, that I think it is an interference with our ability to prepare our Defence in this case, it's not justified in any way that I can see, especially considering the history of this matter, that we were able to have those communications throughout the Pre-Trial without having a co-counsel in Banja Luka. The reason we were not able to do it of course was that our co-counsel who was in Banja Luka was removed from the case and the Registry wouldn't give us any kind of a substitute in order to have that communication. I don't know -- I can't tell you now what future affect that might the have but we've lost a couple of months where at least one of those months there probably could have been significant progress made regarding the preparation of the Defence case. There may be another matter that I'll want to bring to your attention later but that remains to be seen regarding Ms. Jevtovic but I'll bring that to your attention only if it becomes necessary. But I did want to put this issue on the record because I just think that it's an unjustified interference with what we are trying to accomplish in the Defence. Beyond that, Your Honour, that's all I really have to say. I do want to tell you that I'm sorry that my condition caused such a significant delay in this case, especially with the additional delay but it was beyond anyone's control and I made it back here as fast as I could and I think we are able to move forward starting today without any future difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. I can assure you that the Trial Chamber appreciates that because it wasn't just a problem -- it wasn't just your problem. It was also our problem. And we have, as you can imagine, not just an interest but also a responsibility towards the Tribunal in general and this case, which we are charged. With regard to your comments, the Trial Chamber asks the Registrar to communicate to the Registrar, Mr. Holthuis, a copy of the relative part of the transcript. Yes. Mr. Ackerman, I do have some comments to make, some remarks and some questions to put regarding several issues. You're free to go if you want to go. It won't take much time, however. More or less I'm going through what I think is pending so that we will have a picture of -- a clear picture of where we stand before we proceed. There is pending a Prosecution motion regarding to an expert -- one of the expert witnesses. Now, we have decided already the one relating to Mr. Kieser, who I understand will be coming forward next week to give evidence, if my information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right, and we intend to call him properly in any event. I noticed that Your Honours said he had to be here for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When I say "properly," we are going to obviously just highlight the parts of the report where perhaps some clarification would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And yes, I think he is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next week. I'm informed next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is then the other person. We have taken note of your response, Mr. Ackerman, and I have given instructions to my legal officer to prepare a draft which then will need to be discussed with the other two judges, and we should be in a position to hand down the decision by not later than Wednesday. Because it's not going to be a difficult or a lengthy decision. And I don't think it would be controversial. We are not, however, going to grant a hearing because I think that you have dealt with the issues thoroughly already in the -- in a written form and we don't see that we need to spend time in any oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's Mr. Brown you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The military expert. There is another matter which will be decided this week which we have discussed thoroughly and we have agreed upon, and that's with regard to the Prosecution's fresh motion for the subpoena of Jonathan Randal. We will be deciding it again probably Wednesday, latest Thursday, and so that's another matter that has been cooking. And we -- then there is the Prosecution motion for admission of statements under Rule 92 bis related to the Bosanski Petrovac municipality. This is pending. There is also pending the similar motion related to Teslic and another one to Bosanska Krupa. Then there is another Prosecution's motion under -- again under 92 bis related to destruction of religious sites, Celinac, Sipovo, and again another one for Celinac, and then there is a Prosecution 16th motion for protective measures, and another one with regard to Bosanski Petrovac, again Rule 92 bis. These are all pending. My suggestion to the Defence in particular, if there is anything still pending from your side with regard to any of these Rule 92 bis motions, then please put us in a position where we can decide because quite a few of them, and we need to decide them as quickly as possible. I understand that some of them are -- you have responded to some of them but not to all of them, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have responded on Petrovac. With regard to the religious sites, I sent an e-mail to the Prosecutor yesterday. It's not possible for us to respond to that until we have more information from the Prosecutor. I will be working on Teslic today. It's fairly long so it will take me a while. I can tell you with regard to Petrovac that we are not objecting to any of the Prosecutor's Rule 92 proposals; we are accepting them all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you are contesting the documents, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, we have objections to -- the vast majority of the exhibits came from the AID office, which we consider a corrupted source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So please take note of what I've said and I appreciate that you are working on these. Please put us in a position where we can decide them without much delay. Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one further pending - it should have been filed - protective measures motion, in relation to a witness from Celinac -- I'm sorry it should have been filed on Friday but it will be filed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know you're not, but that's where BT90 came from. Secondly, in respect to the documents from Petrovac I must say I thought we had moved beyond AID's forgeries, but does Mr. Ackerman or Ms. Baruch require us to call Mr. Inayat or is it, as it were, the standing objection, because in that case I'll ask Your Honours to make a ruling to admit them subject to the usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the standing objection. It's in writing, it's been filed. It almost all has to do with the source of the documents. There are few of them that have to do with the lack of signatures or stamps or things like that, that just don't even appear to be authentic. It's the collection of documents that is mostly AID documents. It's very different from most other municipalities in that it almost 100 per cent reliance on AID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, then, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then, we will be reaching Petrovac by Wednesday. That's the first witness, and I will then make an application to Your Honours before I call the witness in respect of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And the last perhaps most important thing that I wanted to mention is that I would like you, Ms. Korner, in the course of this week, to work out as precisely as possible a schedule indicating when the Prosecution expects to finish its case. The reason is that we need to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. discuss then whether it's the case of shortening or providing -- so that we make sure that the case of the Prosecution is finalised by a certain date. So if you can work on it and let us have a schedule, a tentative schedule, we will then be in a position to see whether we are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, if I understand Your Honour correctly, Your Honour is saying that you are going to bring down a guillotine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We may have to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which is something I've raised on a number of occasions before. But, Your Honour, we know that this is a matter that has been concerning Your Honours and we have spent certainly the last week since I've been back trying to work this out as best we can. As best we can, we would like to finish the case before the summer break at the beginning of August. And there is a prospect of that. But it is possible that we will have a couple of leftover, maybe one extra witness. So we do anticipate finishing at the latest at the beginning of September. I think we start again on the 25th of August. But, Your Honour, the problem is that had we known in advance, I think, for example, it might be that we would have cut out this particular municipality but we had already started it so we had to finish, and what is coming up now -- and may I make this clear. It did occur to me that obviously as we reach the end of the case, we are going to be hitting experts and major witnesses, the municipality of Kotor Varos is particularly our major municipality. To a certain extent it will depend very much on the ability of the Defence to be able to probably take alternate witnesses, like we do, because we will be running into expert after expert after expert, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, please do work out on this schedule.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've done that. I mean, that is the best we can do. We do hope to finish by the beginning of August, but we have doubts because of the nature of the witnesses that we will be able to complete it all. We have I think some four municipalities left, Petrovac, Krupa -- no, five, actually, Teslic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have Teslic --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, the -- you will appreciate, Ms. Korner, that in these last two months, particularly in this last month, with both Mr. Ackerman and yourself in the position you were in, last thing we would have thought of is to bring you together again and discuss how we could cut down. So it has been on my mind. I have asked my secretary, legal -- not secretary, my legal officer to work out where we could cut down. I do have some suggestions to make, but obviously, I mean, there is no point in even starting discussing these unless you are both present here and you were not both present here, so we had to postpone it. There is still, I think, a solution that could be found, reliance on Rule 92 bis also is one way of cutting down and I do appreciate that you have moved in that direction too. But we need to make sure that, if possible, we finish the Prosecution case entirely certainly before the recess, the summer recess, and if possible, even before. So we'll --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say in terms -- there is no question, but even as Your Honour says, we put as many witnesses as we can as Rule 92, Your Honours then have to rule on any Defence request for cross-examination, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I can say without a shadow of a doubt, there is no prospect of finishing even reducing it to its limited extent even before the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But if that's what Your Honour's order will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll see. You appreciate, Ms. Korner, that we are not in a position to tell you: Drop this municipality or drop that municipality. We will certainly not do that for obvious reasons. But certain measures will have to be taken for sure, and this is why I'm asking you to prepare this tentative schedule because on the basis of that we can really figure it out as we go along. In the meantime, Mr. Ackerman, you would be helping the Trial Chamber considerably if at some point in time, I appreciate it may be a little bit too early for you at this moment, but please do work out in your mind a possible time frame that you will require for your case, just to give us an indication of what to expect. There is a time limit beyond which this trial cannot go, and we have proceeded with -- slowly because of certain problems that we've had so we need to plan ahead much, much more than we would have otherwise had to. All right? So you will come back to us when you can, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we in fact have been trying to do some work on that. I alluded to it in my earlier comments regarding the inability to communicate with Mr. Brdjanin during this period of time, that that kind of gave us a little bit of a set back but we are trying to get that put together. The one kind of fear that I had as I sat here and listened to what you were just talking about, I hope it is not Your Honour's plan to make us use the summer recess as a period of time to prepare our motion and brief regarding no case to answer because that would take away what is treasured vacation time which we really need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman, but it is our plan definitely. We cannot now in the situation in which we find ourselves -- you know, I mean, look at the summer recess as if it is a time of rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's extraordinarily unfair, Your Honour and I object very strongly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Unfortunately we had to stop for two months and I want to know if any other court anywhere in the world which has to stop for two months because of reasons like we had to. I mean, it just doesn't happen, and if it does, then obviously you have to make up for it. We will give due consideration to what will become necessary as we go along, but please don't even think for a moment that the month of August is going to be considered as if it's just a recess in which you can take a whole month off. We just can't afford it at this present moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's what it's for. That's what it is designed for. It recognises that people who work hard need some leisure time, need some vacation time and for you to make me work during that time is just a horrible imposition. If this case ended any other time than when that break was coming up, you wouldn't be able to do that and I just think it's unfair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, we have to finish this case by not later than the 31st of August next year. That's the maximum, because of the ad litem Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think there is any problem getting that done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You think so, but I also never thought that we would have had to stop for two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I didn't get cancer on purpose and I haven't been on vacation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know that, Mr. Ackerman. I know that, Mr. Ackerman. And you also know that we could have taken other steps because as I said, had it happened to me, I would have been asked to resign straight away. Because this Tribunal could not afford to have a trial stop because one of the judges is sick for two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's happened before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, it hasn't happened before. There is no other case that had to stop for two months because one of the judges was sick. I appreciate your situation, and we did our best to preserve your presence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, and I guess it's now -- well, I won't say that, it wouldn't be wise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's -- exactly. I think we better leave it at that. We will take it up as we go along, but please don't expect us to say August will be free for everyone and you can relax. We will be working in August. I was working in August last year. But I had to come Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. back because of certain work that urgent work that came up here and cut short my holidays. So -- but any way, we will discuss it later, Mr. Ackerman. So that's the position, and we'll wait this tentative schedule from you, Ms. Korner. Ms. Korner

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please try to have available this tentative schedule in the course of this week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Time frame more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think Your Honours were sent a sort of list of anticipated witnesses, weren't you? Yes. Which shows roughly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have a list of anticipated witnesses until the 27th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's all I have. I have it here in front of me and it's order of witnesses for the month of May and June 2003. But that's as far as I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, yes, we'll see what we can do. As I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is no Kotor Varos here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. We are starting Kotor Varos in July. But, Your Honour, I have heard what Your Honours have said well in mind and we'll just have to see what we can do. As I say, we would prefer also to complete by the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner and Mr. Ackerman, you have to understand that we are now in a position where one needs to leave time for two very important decisions that this Trial Chamber will have to hand down. One is immediately after you finish the case for the Prosecution and then at the end, for the final judgement, right? So we are talking of two periods of time which -- one of which, the latter, in particular, in a case like this, would -- one would expect to last for at least three months, easily, easily. There is the case, the Defence case, that I don't know how long it's going to take but we need to take that into consideration and give maximum allowance for that. And we need to finish by not later than August of next year. So if there is a major calamity like we have had, we have a problem. So I have worked it out in my mind with the assistance of my staff, there is an allowance, a margin, of a couple of months. If we have a calamity, we have a problem. And this is why we will have to take certain steps because I want to make sure that there is a wider margin, enough, not to put any pressure on anyone and at the same time to release the pre-occupation that we have that we -- that the case may come to a halt. I mean, please do appreciate that. We have a responsibility. We will try to accommodate each one of you as much as we could, but at the same time we can't work miracles and we can't allow the case to come to a halt. So this is the position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make one more suggestion? And that's this: We are supposed to be boxing and coxing with the case of Krajisnik. As Your Honour and I think everybody knows that's not started and may not start for some weeks at the present rate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if we could make full use then of the Court that's available by perhaps sitting a little longer, by sitting a day as opposed to the half days like this? I think that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly have nothing against it and I would be all for it. I don't want to put undue pressure on --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think it depends very much when Mr. Ackerman's new co-counsel feels that he'll be in a position to take full part in the case. But, Your Honour, that's a suggestion that I have because I think that would really speed matters up because we could call, with luck, two witnesses a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you agree on that now, I can give instructions straight away to the Registrar to work out a different schedule, court schedule, for the next month and a half because I don't anticipate Krajisnik starting before a month and a half, and we could do that. But I need the consent of both of you at this point in time before I proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand that, and so I'm merely raising that suggestion and obviously, it would have to be from next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason I say it, Ms. Korner, is this: That Mr. Ackerman has no problem between now and the end of May, because there is Mrs. Baruch and Mr. Cunningham here who can take over. But starting on the 1st of June, if everything goes as expected, Mr. Ackerman will be back in the courtroom and -- I don't want to -- I don't know what the situation is going to be. I mean, maybe okay for him to be here whole morning or a whole afternoon but quite an inconvenience to be here from 9.00 in the morning until --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I was thinking something like Milosevic hours, Your Honour, which is 9.30 or whatever until 3, but that would certainly give us extra time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, he's heard what has been said, he will think about it, and when he's in a position to let us know, then we'll decide accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's impossible for me to know exactly how I'm going to feel two weeks from now. I seem to be getting a little bit stronger every day, but I'm good for about four or five hours a day now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I have gone through this before with relatives of mine. The moment you overdo it, you'll pay for it, okay? So this is why I'm saying August, my idea is to work in August, work not here in the courtroom but my idea is to work in August. But obviously we will have to reconsider the position as it obtains -- as it will obtain at the time and take the appropriate decision, but here and now it's not my intention to waste August as if it's just an entire month or three weeks off. That's my suggestion at the present moment. We will talk about it. August is still pretty much far away, while the 1st of June is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you will feel certainly better at the end of July than you would feel in the beginning of June. So at this point in time, I don't expect you to give me an answer. We will talk about it. I don't know, perhaps we could --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no objection starting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Lengthen -- yeah --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have no objection starting the month of June with some extended hours if you want to try that, with the understanding that I might stand up and say, "Judge, I can't go any further today." I mean, that could happen but I think we might as well try to set up the schedule so we can do it if we can do it. It makes sense to me. I feel a need because of -- I assume, Your Honour, that when you're saying we have to finish by August of next year, what you're -- what you mean is that we have to have final judgement by August of next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, the term of offers of the two ad litem Judges expires definitely without the possibility of an extension the end of August of next year.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, all of us need to cooperate to do our best to make that work, Your Honour, and I think we probably can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise what it means is that the trial starts again for whatever that involves, as far as your client is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do need to just point out for the record that the process of preparing the Defence case has been repeatedly interfered with. First of all, my first co-counsel was suspended, who was the person who knew the most about this case, and we would be way along the road for preparation if she had been able to stay on the case. Then my second co-counsel whose job -- whose assignment was to get the Defence case Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. prepared and that's what he was working on. He was removed. The third person who has knowledge about this matter and who now has taken over responsibility for doing that work and getting that case prepared is Ms. Jevtovic who the Registry has now told me will be removed as of June 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ackerman, let's cut this short. You're allergic to bananas and you eat a banana and you get a rash, it's only your fault. You shouldn't have eaten the banana. Don't let me start on commenting and remarking on your choice of co-counsel as we have been going along on this case. So I have my strong reservations on the choice of the co-counsel in each case. And the least said about this is better. Maybe you don't agree with what I am saying, but the end result is measures had to be taken as we went along, precisely because there was something wrong each time with the choice of the co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But they are now saying they are going to remove Ms. Jevtovic and there is nothing wrong with her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ackerman, having someone come here one day and the next day she decides that she doesn't want even to turn up or have the decency, you have -- you wouldn't be able to do that. You would never dream of doing that because you know that there is a rule of ethics that doesn't allow you to do that. Even if you are sacked, even if a co-counsel is sacked, the Registrar will impose on that co-counsel a time limit during which he has or she has to stay here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me make it very clear what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the most offensive behaviour imaginable for someone to decide here and now to abandon the client, abandon you, abandon everyone simply because there is a misunderstanding or there is lack of agreement or dissatisfaction with the amount that she is being paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Judge, you misunderstand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't care, Mr. Ackerman. But I would not accept, tolerate, anyone to behave the way she did behave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I do. You do misunderstand and I care that you do understand properly. What they did -- she had an agreement with regard to compensation. She came here under that agreement. All of a sudden, the Registry announced they were cutting her remuneration in half. She had a contract, my view is, to perform services for a certain amount.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, there are ways and means and there are ethical rules that need to be observed by everyone. I know that you observe scrupulously also because you are the president of the lawyer's association here, the Defence association, but that's not the way to go about it. And anyone who can abandon everyone else, the client, the lead counsel, the co-counsel, and fail to turn up, leaving everyone in the lurch, unable to start the sitting because we have to find a replacement, temporary replacement even to be able to provide interpretation and a direct link between you and your client, that's unheard of. I mean, I would never tolerate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a very long period of time when I negotiated with the Registry on her behalf, argued with the Registry on her behalf, I wrote a letter to Your Honours explaining what was going on, asking you to assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we assisted you, but the result was that the moment she decided she was important to enough to walk out on us, she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I was then finally able to convince her that that was a mistake and that she should remain, and she decided to remain under the conditions that the Registry was now imposing upon her and after then she had decided to remain under the conditions the Registry wanted her to remain under, they then sent me a letter saying they are going to sack her in any event. You know, regardless, it just puts a great big hole in our ability to do this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ackerman, you as lead counsel, you have a responsibility. I wouldn't like to have someone -- if I were lead counsel instead of you, I wouldn't like to live with the uncertainty that such an assistant provides, basing on the past experience. Anyone who walks out on me like that, without prior notice, you looked very surprised when you walked in the courtroom that day, telling us what happened, she's just left, she decided to abandon the case. You can't accept that. Yes. Judge Taya is telling me to proceed. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are you ready to bring the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can I be excused then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, Mr. Ackerman. And not even an apology. She came back into the courtroom

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So how are we going to proceed now with the facial distortion and --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The same technical requirement has been met, I think, and there are no people allowed to sit in the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what about transmission?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we need to go into private session when he comes in, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session. One moment then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are not going to show the face.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the important thing, that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a moment, sir, you're going to be handed a map and I want to ask you some questions. You can put that on the ELMO, please. Now, sir, we can see marked on that map the village of Lisnja. You've told us there were about three and a half thousand people living there. Of what nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims, Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The villages that surround it, were they also Bosniak villages or were they Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The villages around Lisnja were all Serbian villages, and then further on, there were Galjipoljci and Vrbovci and then there were some Bosniaks living in Prnjavor as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the village of Lisnja, did that have a commune or was that part of a commune?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lisnja was or constituted a local commune.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not marked on the map but was there a village call Milosavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And that was part of the local commune of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nationality of the persons who lived in that village of Milosavci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there in Lisnja a mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And within the town or within the village of Lisnja, were there any military barracks or structures or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you knew, was there any military importance to the village of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Lisnja form part of a -- or did it have a TO unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was in 1995. A TO unit was established within the TO of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's been translated as in 1995. Do you mean 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not then. Lisnja was empty in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note. I believe that the witness in fact said 1991, but if you want you can check with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The interpreter --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say 1991, there was a TO unit established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around that time. I don't know the exact date. I am just saying Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that that was the approximate time it was established, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you a member of that TO unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of what nationality was the commander of the TO unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Was there a police station in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There wasn't one. However, a patrol was established at around that time. Perhaps a bit after the TO unit was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did the patrol come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some were from Lisnja, some from Milosavci, and I think that an active policeman used to come from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who was in charge of that police patrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that was the policeman from Prnjavor who used to come. He was in charge of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move to the events of 1991 and 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I go into private session for just a short part of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, during this period from the time of the war in Croatia up until the events of April/May of 1992, were you aware of people being dismissed from their employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was. It was in the media. I used to come across people who had been fired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were being fired, of what nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly Bosniaks and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What reason was given for them losing their jobs, usually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Based on what I knew, the major reason was that they would be mobilised or issued call-up papers to go to war in Croatia. They would fail to respond and be fired as a result.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about women? Were they being fired as well, Bosniak women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Perhaps a bit later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the -- if people, Bosniaks, were fired, did that affect their accommodation in some cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps not right away, but sometime later they would lose their accommodation, some people would, or at least most of them lost their housing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those who had lost their housing, where would they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they managed, they would stay with friends, relatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a stage, and if you can remember roughly when that started, when people, Bosniaks, and Croats, were forcibly evicted from their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only heard about that. I heard that they had been evicted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From those whom you spoke to, how had those evictions taken place? What had actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually uniformed people would come, mostly those who had fought in war in Croatia. I don't know whether they did it arbitrarily or not, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware whether any complaint was made to the authorities about these evictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably yes. They complained and they were told that things would be taken care of and that it would be investigated, and as to who was responsible and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are aware, was any action taken by the authorities to reinstate, put back into their accommodation, the people who had been evicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. There were some attempts. There were even conflicts breaking out between the police and these troops. I don't know what to call them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to next move to politicians. Did you have a television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see politicians appearing on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Radoslav Brdjanin on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know what position he held at the time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I truly don't know, but he was in the top echelons in Banja Luka, and since we were a bit away, I didn't know exactly what office he held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ask him whether he would be in a position to recognise Mr. Brdjanin to start with and whether he sees him in this courtroom, if he can recognise him in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think I'll wait to see if there is an objection to that. I don't think we have done that so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since you are addressing him precisely as to -- on the subject and he's telling you that he saw Radoslav Brdjanin, I want to know which Radoslav Brdjanin he saw on TV, whether he can recognise him here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be able to recognise Mr. Brdjanin now, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I would, if I looked around, perhaps. I think that the gentleman is sitting all the way in the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think perhaps for the purposes of the note, we better have a more accurate description.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anybody sitting next to him that you can see, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see, but there is a policeman there, I think it's a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, unless there is an objection, clearly he's identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I know this is some years ago, sir, now, but can you remember what he was saying, what his speeches were like that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. All I can say was that he delivered those speeches in an energetic way but I can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not asking for the details, sir, but generally speaking, can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you remember what he was saying about the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said that non-Serbs need to be moved out, this needs to be done, that needs to be done, just like what other politicians used to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember, and if you can't, sir, say straight away, roughly -- from roughly what period you first saw him on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to move now to the actual events, so perhaps -- I know it's a little early but we can have the break now and I can move to the events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We can have the break now. Do you need time -- 25 minutes will be enough? So 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should say the Defence were aware of what the witness was going to say about Mr. Brdjanin. I informed them of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope so. So we'll have a break of 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, bringing in the witness, we go into -- make sure that all precautions are taken, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, just before we bring back the witness, mention this? Your Honours will now see Mr. Nicholls is here instead of Ms. Sutherland, and he's calling the next witness who is here and available. I estimate to be about another hour in chief. Your Honour, the real question is whether we want to get him brought here with the possibility of starting today. Can I say straight away that the witness from Petrovac does not arrive until this evening, so he can't testify until Wednesday. Mr. Nicholls's witness will certainly finish in one day, just like this one. So I'm wondering whether it's worth bringing him here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It all depends on how long the cross-examination will last. I hate to ask actually because -- I hate to ask you how long you expect your cross-examination to last because the examination-if-chief hasn't finished as yet, so you never know what might come out. Could we have an estimate, Ms. Baruch, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Another difficulty.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Besides not knowing how long the direct examination will be, Your Honour, we spent a great deal of this morning on other matters, which I know we will not do in the afternoon or I don't believe we do. I did an extensive preparation on this particular witness. I can tell you that I have 19 pages of questions but they are double-spaced, large words, large printing, and I've never had the experience of waiting for interpreters and then hearing the witness. I'll be better prepared to answer such a question the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I would suggest you keep the other witness where he is and we'll bring him over tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Baruch. So let's go ahead. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to now move to the events in April/May of 1992. Did there come a time when there was a demand for the surrender of weapons in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you become aware of that demand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First the request was made to surrender hunting rifles through the delegates. There was a notification for the hunting rifles to be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, who was it who was saying that hunting rifles had to be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know their names, but in any case, the whole village was aware of that demand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that, sorry, I don't want the names but which authorities were saying you, the villagers, had to surrender your hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An order came from the municipality but I don't know which body was in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And you heard about it from, you said, the delegates. Were those delegates from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the surrender of hunting rifles, were those licensed rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself own a hunting rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you were all informed of this demand, was there a meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There were no meetings. On the day when the weapons were to be surrendered, a lot of people gathered, we were all there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you gather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of the cultural centre, the culture hall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did -- as far as you were aware, did most of the men in the village go to the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were men, women, children. It was a spontaneous thing. There was no danger in all that, no harm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was decided about the surrender of the weapons? Was the agreement to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some people surrendered their weapons immediately. There was a team from Prnjavor who received the weapons and some on the other hand did not want to surrender their weapons. So those who had surrendered their weapons influenced the others, told them, surrender your weapons, let's avoid any problems, and they found a lorry and the remainder of the weapons were then subsequently taken to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who didn't want to surrender their weapons, what was the reason behind that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know why they didn't, how come they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those of you who did surrender -- not you personally but those who did surrender their weapons, why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most probably to avoid problems. They understood that as an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from hunting rifles, were you aware that anyone in Lisnja had other weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Such as?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I can't -- there were rifles, mostly light arms, pistols, rifles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day. A request had not been made to surrender that kind of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those sort of weapons, were they personal weapons or were they part of the TO weaponry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of it belonged to the Territorial Defence but there were some personal weapons as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, at any stage, did your -- did the village of Lisnja suggest to the authorities that they were not -- that they were going to resist any attempt to disarm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The relationships were good between the local commune and the authorities in Prnjavor. The relationships were okay, I would say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had there been any attempt by the village of Lisnja to set up barricades to stop people coming into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you say some of the weapons were surrendered to the people who came from Prnjavor and others were later collected in a truck and taken to Prnjavor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once these weapons had been taken, did anybody arrive in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe five or ten minutes - I can't give you the exact time - some soldiers came in a lorry. They drove through the entire village, they started cursing us, they started telling us: Why did you surrender those weapons? We are here to kill you because you surrendered your weapons. There was no violence. They just drove through the village, they were shooting in the air, and they were cursing us, they used derogatory terms to address us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These soldiers, were you able to identify what kind of soldiers they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as White Eagles. They had patches on one side, and they had gloves with no fingers, they had balaclavas or masks on their faces. I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have, you say, patches on one side. Was there anything on the patches, any insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, there were patches or insignia in the shape of an eagle or something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say that they drove through the village, they were firing, and they wanted to know why you'd surrendered your weapons, as they wanted to -- as they were here to kill you. Did anything happen apart from that? Did they stop at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They did not. As far as I could see, and according to the stories that I heard, they didn't stop. They just drove straight through the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself saw them, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did see them in that lorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did all this display make you and your co-villagers feel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were all upset and it was a very unpleasant sight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after that, did there come a time when some police officers came looking for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was after some time. I don't know when this happened. I believe it was on the 27 or on the 28th of May, a police patrol came, consisting of four or five men. They came looking for me and some other people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see those police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my neighbour's courtyard and I saw them entering my front yard, and I heard them inquiring about me, and then I just ran away. I fled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did you run away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was afraid. We would all run away before a foot soldier, before any car. You -- it was -- you were better off hiding because you never knew who might that be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what was it that made you afraid? What did you think might happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People were being taken away. This person was taken from here, that person was taken from there. It was not just the authorities that came. There were other people, people who would put on uniforms, just, you know, ordinary people putting on uniforms. You really didn't know who they were and that's why we were all afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these police officers and the people who would suddenly put on uniforms, what nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no way of knowing. They would come to the village, they would not introduce themselves, they wore uniforms, they could be anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with the police officers who came to your house that day. Before you ran away, were you able to recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that the leader of that patrol was Dragan Mehtic who talked to my wife, asked where I was, asked her to come look for me, and when he didn't find me, he left a message with her that I should report to -- for an interview, for an interrogation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You say, I believe it was Dragan Mehtic because you saw him or because you were told so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had never seen him in a uniform before but I knew him and I saw a tall guy and I thought I recognised him, and also they told me that I should report to him, to Dragan, when I went to Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was any reason given to your wife as to why you should report to Prnjavor for an interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They just told me I should go for an interview, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just go into private session, Your Honour, for the next couple of questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go to private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you'd been ordered to report to the police station in Prnjavor, so did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did, together with somebody else they wanted to report for an interview. Since my children had left already, we decided that he wouldn't go, that he would stay, he was an active member of the SDA. I went there, it was Saturday, I reported to the duty operations officer, he didn't have a clue. He said: Well, who asked you to come? And I said: Well, I'm to report to Dragan, and then Dragan came in civilian clothes and Dragan told me: Go home, come back on Monday, we will continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go back on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, I believe, the 1st of June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went back to the police station, on that occasion, were you questioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They put me in a room, I waited there, then I talked to one person, to another person, they asked me whether I was a member, I said yes, no, you're lying, you're not lying, who has weapons, who hasn't? So there was no ill treatment. It was just a simple conversation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, whilst you were at the police station on that Monday, the 1st of June, did you notice anything happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime around -- I don't know how late it was, I noticed some sort of preparations going on at the police station, and then all of a sudden everything quieted down for a couple of hours I was on my own, nobody came to me, nobody asked me anything, nobody talked to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you kept at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there all the time in that one room, and then in the late afternoon, they came and brought me downstairs to the ground floor, and there I saw two other men from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you just give us their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Senijad Mujanic was there and Gusic. The second person was just sort of, just passing through. He was released pretty quickly. I gave him the key to my car because I'd come by car and I asked him to take my car home and he did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment. Could you just tell us the name of the second man again who you gave your car keys to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zinaid Gusic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So were you -- did you and Mr. Mujanic remain in the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did. But we could not talk to each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you kept at the police station overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact times, because I also heard at the time that something was going on in Lisnja regarding the surrender of weapons. On Monday morning, nobody knew anything about any surrender of weapons. At least I didn't know. Maybe others did. It was an order that came out of the blue sky, and then there was something they called an armed rebellion and villagers did not fire any arms. I don't know what was going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll come on to that in a moment. But can we just deal with your position? Were you kept at the police station overnight or were you moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were moved. I was put in one part of the building and Mujanic was put in another part of the building, but I believe it was on the subsequent day, I believe that we spent the night on the ground floor but I can't say that for a fact. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were there other people that you knew being kept at the police station, whom you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand. What people do you have in mind when you ask me that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you saw or you were taken out past another cell in that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. While I was staying in that room or in that cell, I didn't know what the time was or anything, but next to that cell, there was a kindergarten and I could hear children playing so I assumed it was still daylight. At one point the door opened and the policeman who opened the door asked me: What are you doing here? Why are you here? And I said: I don't know. Dragan had been interrogating me and that's where we left it off. And then a Serbian soldier entered the cell. He was from the neighbouring village. And again asked me why am I hear? And I asked him: Why are you here? And he says: I killed my brother. He was in the neighbouring cell. And then after half an hour, again the door opened and they took me to have a drink of water, they gave me a sandwich. As I was walking through that passage to the public security station to drink water, I saw a cell with the door open and I saw a number of people from my village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, the people that you saw from your village, were you able to talk to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you eventually taken to the cultural centre in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I had had a sandwich and a drink of water, I returned to the cell, I didn't stay there long, a policeman came, opened the door, and told me: We are taking you to the cultural centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And when you were taken to the cultural centre, were there other people already there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The centre was packed. There were people from Lisnja, from my village, there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from them what had happened in Lisnja that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. First I came across the people who were from Puraci, that's a hamlet next to Lisnja and they told me what had happened, that there had been shelling, that there were dead people lying around. And I asked where my neighbours were, and then they told me that they were on the far end of the cultural sent are by the stage. That's where I found them. We talked, and they told me that the houses had been set fire to and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all the people that you saw in the cultural centre men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they all adult men or were there young boys there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a few young boys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you kept at the Dom Kultura, the culture centre, for some days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, 200, 300, maybe more. I can't give you the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there beds or any sleeping arrangements for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was nothing there, just the floor. We spent a day or two days there. I don't know. And then on one occasion, Veljko Milankovic came. I don't know what his rank was, but in any case, he had his own paramilitary unit, and he asked the policemen: Why do you keep these people like that? Why don't you give them food, water, beds? And the policemen obeyed him immediately we were given water, sandwiches, and then he addressed all of us and he said, "There won't be any problems. I'll deal with this. I'll see what this is all about." He spoke along these lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I want to come back to him in a moment but before he arrived, had you been given any food or water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were police officers there. The regular policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say Milankovic arrived. Had you ever met Milankovic before this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him. I knew him. I didn't know him personally, but I knew who he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was he, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, he was, how shall I put it, he was a criminal, he did all sorts of dodgy things. He had been convicted felon. He did all sorts of things. He had been tried and sentenced for various crimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he had his own paramilitary unit. Do you know what that unit was called?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he had a paramilitary unit. Do you know what that unit was called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We all know that. They were Wolves from Vucjak. That's what they were called. Because he was a native of Vucjak. He was born in the vicinity and that's why his paramilitary units was called like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he arrived at the cultural centre, was he in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he -- well, he was wearing civilian clothes, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were shown by the investigator a copy of a photograph and I'd like you to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have obtained the original because the copies that I think we all have are terribly bad. It's also a photocopy but we'll get a better one done so we will hand them out later rather than making this an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you just look at that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you put it on the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the man that you knew as Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that a copy be made an exhibit. It will be P1781 but we'll give a better copy to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you ever notice the insignia that -- when you'd seen Milankovic before was on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a wolf's head. I don't know on which arm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now again you were shown a photograph of such insignia by the investigator. Could you have a look at that, please. Is that the insignia that was on the uniforms of those called the wolves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a head. That was something like that but there was also an inscription, Wolves from Vucjak. I can't see whether this is written here or not. The head is similar but I don't know whether the mouth was actually open or not. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be made - again we will get a better copy for the Registry - P1782? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that he arrived and he told the police officers or he told you, I think, that you'd get food and water; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he actually, in your presence, tell police officers that you were to be provided with food and water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He did, in our presence, he said it outloud, all of us were present when he said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you surprised when he said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were truly surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him arrive, what did you think was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We thought the worst would happen. However, things took a different turn, and it was fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after he had been there, you told us that the police did in fact give you food and water.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did give us food and sandwiches. They treated us well. Things were great right then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that you found your neighbours and they told you what had happened to Lisnja. Did you discover what had happened to your family? Your wife and children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were in Prnjavor. They were safe with family and relatives, and the entire village of Lisnja spent several days in Prnjavor, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "the entire," what, every male -- man, woman and child left Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, perhaps some had remained, 5 to 10 per cent; however, I wasn't there so I can't say. Most were outside of the village, in Prnjavor, with family and so on. They had no trouble finding accommodation with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And did you see your family while you were still at the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After Milankovic's visit, some other people whom I don't know came as well. They decided to allow us five, ten minutes, or three minutes for talking to our families in the presence of the police. They allowed us to have that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after that, were you taken from the Dom Kultura -- from the cultural centre to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to the former shoe factory, Sloga. There was a plant there, and they put us in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that all the persons who had been kept, detained, in the cultural centre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you were asked by the investigator to draw a sketch of the Sloga factory, the inside. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you be shown that, please? Now, can you just tell us what you were indicating in that sketch? If you can do it on the -- on there, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The entrance gate was here and you can't see the fence on the sketch but it was there. Then this is the yard, the entrance, and then one entered the first room. That was the first room where all of us were initially. And then the door was here, and the entrance to the second room. This door was closed off. And somewhere here there was another building, and there were toilets there and water facilities. One would leave the room, go through the yard to get to these facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there were two rooms, were there, in which you and the other people were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Initially all of us were in this one room, because this door was closed off and the second room was empty. So for the first few days, all of us were in this first room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have an indication of the size of this first room where they were altogether initially, please? Roughly in square metres? Was it -- let's start from here. Was it bigger than this hall that you're in now?
