utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps wider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps wider.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And again how many people roughly were in that room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there room for you all to lie down at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. Some would lie and some would stand up. We would take turns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did they keep all of you in that one room for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps two or three days, and then they let us go into the second room, and they allowed our family members to bring in bed linen, food from home, and so on. And then after some seven -- or during some seven to eight days they would always escort us when we needed to go to the toilets. Later on we were allowed to go unescorted. They would just let us walk freely in the yard. So conditions improved on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were, the group that you were with were all put into that one room. At a later stage, were other people brought to the factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Other people were brought in, and once other people were brought in, they allowed us to use the second room, and they moved us around, and then after ten to 15 days or perhaps less they started releasing people. Initially, they would release the minors and then the seniors, and then people would be released every week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the people who were there, what ethnicity were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Croats living in your area at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but in the area of your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Lisnja. In the surrounding area there were some people of Polish, Ukrainian ethnicity and then the rest were all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally on that, all the people who had been kept at Sloga were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that sketch be made P1783, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you take note of that, Madam Registrar, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That we can hand in because the copy is fairly clear. You can take it away now, thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whilst you were at the Sloga factory, were interrogations carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were interrogations. There were, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the interrogations carried out in the factory itself or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Occasionally in the factory but mostly in the premises of MUP or SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you like this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you like this, but two things actually. This has been put on the ELMO and it contains -- at least the copy that I am given it contains the witness's initials. I don't know if you care for that or not. Second question is whether it should be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, it should be tendered under seal, I feel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it was on the ELMO, it's too late now to do anything about anyhow so -- thank you, Your Honour, for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it will be tendered and accepted under seal, Madam Registrar, please, thank you, and I did something wrong with my monitor or -- it's yours, too?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, actually I suppose as is there is delayed transmission, perhaps we can just edit the transmission to cover that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we could do that. I don't know whether technically that is possible but I suppose it is. First of all, we have lost -- I have lost my monitor completely. I'm not seeing anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you press it again, Your Honour, that's what ours did but it came back again if you press "transcript." No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have yours? Yeah, it came back. Mine came back. Judge Taya? Yeah, it's come back as well. All right. We are okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were telling us about interrogations. You said some at the Sloga, others you said at the premises of the SUP or the MUP. Were you taken out for interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly in the SUP premises. Sometimes for brief periods of time in another place but mostly in SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was doing the interrogating, local police officers or other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes locals, and on two or three occasions, people from Banja Luka, though used to call it DB, state security or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we suspend the sitting for two minutes, please? I need to go out and come back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. --- Break taken at 11.40 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we were talking, I was asking you about the interrogations. How did you know that these people from Banja Luka, the state security, came from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While the local policemen drove to us the site, they would always warn us that these would be people from Banja Luka. That's how I knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what sort of questions were they asking you? What did they want to know, apparently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were interested in everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We lost our monitor again. This is the second time that it's happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Court maintenance on Friday, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I know that. We'll proceed on the laptop. It's come back anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said they were interested in everything but what sort of questions were they asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were asking first about the SDA, green berets, this and that, weapons, what we thought about things, do you know what state you're living in, and things like that. Mostly provocative questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they suggesting that you personally had done anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing particular. They questioned us about everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say they questioned you about weapons. What sort of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They asked about who had weapons, what kind of weapons. They asked whether we were preparing for combat, whether we were organisation -- whether we were organising it and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What replies were you giving to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes we would say, I don't know. If we knew an answer we would give it to them. That's how it went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever admit to being involved in organising armed combat, resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't admit to something where I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did anything ever happen to you during the course of these interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on one occasion, when I was interrogated, the interrogator was a different man, and he told me that I drove some member of the SDA to Sarajevo, which was true, because I went to Sarajevo to visit my sister and the man asked me whether he could come along and I said yes, and we went to Sarajevo, we came back, and that was the end of it. I returned back to the Sloga. The first policeman that interrogated me called me over and asked me: Why were you lying? What didn't you tell me that you were a member of the SDA because I heard what you said later on? And then he told me to lean against the wall and he took a rifle and started hitting me with it, and then he took something else into his hands and hit me a couple of times, and then he told me to leave. I didn't comment. I didn't make any comments while I was in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was happening at the Sloga, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the Sloga.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you as the result of the beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in pain, and I had difficulty moving about, but I believe that those consequences were not grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you, did that happen to other people -- I'm sorry, were other people taken, who were taken for interrogation, also beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, another person was, and -- another person was beaten and that was in the SUP building, and then another person was beaten at the Sloga, not by the interrogator but rather by a policeman who guarded us from time to time. Then one evening, he came in and he hit the man with a pistol on his face, and then the others called the ambulance and took him to the hospital. And then later on, the policeman came in and apologised, saying that he was drunk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how long did you remain as a prisoner at the Sloga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We remained at the Sloga until the 14th of September. I couldn't tell you what date it was when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you spent there, were you ever told why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several times, the then chief of police, Radoslav Vasic, I believe his name was, came to see us. He told us that we were sort of guarded there, to prevent anything bad happening to us. He encouraged us on those occasions, told us we shouldn't be afraid, and told us that as long as civilian authorities were in power, then things were fine. However, once the military takes over the power, then I can't say what's going to happen. So he used to calm us down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he mention any other camps to you, when he was talking about the civilian authorities being in power and things were fine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he would stay maybe half an hour or more, talking to us. We would put questions to him and so on. He would always encourage us and say, "This is great. Nothing bad is going to happen to you. Things are much worse in Prijedor and Doboj," and I don't know what other places he was mentioning. I've forgotten it now. We are doing our best to protect you here. That's what he was saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from him about any particular military camp in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from him, but from others, from the local policemen who were guards there, used to tell us that conditions were great in our camp compared to other camps. They used to mention Derventa Logor, and some other camp -- and some other camps that I didn't see. And they used to tell us that our camp was fantastic compared to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that he mentioned something Logo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They call it Derventa camp, Derventa Logor, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: According to what they state -- according to what they said, there was an estate there, a farm there, and the camp was located on that estate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it have a name, apart from Derventa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's all I heard. I don't know anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where that was, roughly? Where they told you that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know where the horse stable is, where that farm is. However, the exact location, I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How close to the town of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of kilometres, 2 or 3, not far from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they -- did the police officers who were telling you about this, tell you who was being held there and what the conditions were like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They didn't mention anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you were told that you were being kept in the Sloga effectively for your own protection. Did you do anything --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Were you ever taken before a court in Banja Luka or elsewhere and charged with any crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally was not. However, there were some papers received to the effect that we would be transferred to another camp and so on. However, we remained in Sloga and we hired an attorney. I couldn't tell you exactly how many of us got together to hire this attorney, and on one day, they came and took eight or ten people to a prison in Banja Luka, and all of us who had hired an attorney remained at the Sloga without any explanation whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. First of all, a number of you, eight or -- a number of you hired an attorney. How much did each of you have to pay the attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We gave an advance of a thousand Deutschmarks each initially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you hire originally as your attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The attorney was called Petko Vincic. I don't know whether Petko was his first name or his nickname, however his last name was definitely Vincic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe he was a Serb. However he was married to a Muslim woman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were still at the Sloga, perhaps a month had passed by, I couldn't tell you exactly, however he was killed by a Serb soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to have a look at a document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I think we need to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you told us that you were kept in the Sloga factory until the 14th of September. On that day, was the factory closed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, two buses were organised to come and pick us up. There were between 70 and 100 of us there and the others had been released gradually before that. We were taken to the village. They gave us a day or two to rest and then we all had to go to the work obligation. And this lasted up to the time we eventually left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you already had to start the work obligation while you were being kept at Sloga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We started to do our work obligation. We were taken from the Sloga to the fish farm or to Milankovic's estate where we had to do some things, or we would do felling in the forest, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- part of the work obligation was to work on Veljko Milankovic's property, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go back to the village of Lisnja then, after you were released from Sloga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sort of state was it in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the meantime, while I was still there, my father was still alive, and he covered the bits that had been burned out so that they could actually inhabit that house. Most of the houses were burned and my house is, as it was at the -- at that time to this very day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You described your house. I want to talk about the village generally for a moment. You told us that it contained about 3.000 people, roughly how many houses? I don't expect an exact figure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 700 and a thousand, roughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Houses or people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Houses, households, I don't know how I should put it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So you're saying there were something like 700 to a thousand houses as well? Actual buildings is what I mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actual buildings, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got back there, how many of them had been destroyed, roughly? Not an exact figure again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between 80 and 100. At the beginning, some of them were destroyed initially in the first wave, and later on some more were destroyed, but in any case, between 80 and 100 houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Destroyed by shelling or by later destruction, either explosives or setting the houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some houses, a couple of them, were destroyed by shelling. I don't know how many shells actually fell on the village. A few maybe. And the rest were destroyed by subsequent explosions, they were set fire to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about property that remained after the shelling or the destruction? Was all your property there that wasn't destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the actual building is concerned, it was there, but things had been taken from the houses. Some -- from some houses, more things were taken; from some, fewer things were taken. It depended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in comparison to the houses, the majority of the houses in the village, was yours an average size or bigger than most or smaller?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mine was of an average size.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that your father had remained and had done some repairs to it before you came back. What had actually been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The outbuildings were destroyed. It was some 20 metres long or even longer. This was set fire to and it was, since this outbuilding was connected with the house, the -- one part of the roof also burned down and we repaired that part of the roof and the rest is as it was at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to have a look, please, at a document already exhibited, which is P657.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's in the bundle, Your Honours. We've got another copy here. We can hand it up. Put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report, a military report, which you won't have seen but I want to ask for your comment on one aspect of it. It states it's dated the 2nd of June and it states that "In Lisnja village, an armed conflict occurred between Muslim extremists and the army of the Serbian Republic. Some of the Muslim extremists were captured while a rather large number of them pulled out towards Crni VRH." Now, I know that you were in the police station when the attack took place, but before you left, and this is on the 1st of June, as far as you were aware, was anybody in your village armed? Was there any armed unit of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was never any sort of unit there, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It states that some of the Muslim extremists were captured. You have told us that when you got to the cultural hall there were other people there from your village there and others arrived. Were any of them in uniform of any kind or, as far as you knew, any of them take part in any fighting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody took part in anything. I don't know what was going on on that day because I wasn't there but in any case, no resistance was put up, there was no fire opened. That's what I heard. People were telling me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then if you look, please, at paragraph 2, at the end of that paragraph, it states, it's the part beginning in the area of Derventa. It says, "The Muslim population of the area of Lisnja village has been expelled." Would you agree with that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not a classical expulsion. Again I repeat I was not there. They just withdrew to a sawmill some 1 or 2 kilometres away. That's where they spent the night. And on the following morning, women and children went back home. The men had already been taken to Prnjavor and that's how it all ended. This lasted for a couple of hours maybe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And then finally, on the village, you've told us there was a mosque in your village. When you got back there in September, was that mosque still standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then finally, sir, and this is the last question, I think in January of 1993, you sent your children for (Redacted) is that correct? I'm sorry, your children and the rest of your family had already left for (Redacted)is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three days before these developments, my children did indeed go to Germany. My father and my wife remained. When I arrived when I was released from the Sloga, maybe some ten or 15 days later, my wife and my father left, and finally I left the village on the 18th of January to go to Germany as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, sir. That's all the questions I have for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So shall we have a break now? 20 minutes. 25 minutes? 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter before cross-examination, and the defendant -- the accused has to come in. We just picked up Mr. Ackerman's motion objecting to the exhibits in Petrovac. At the end it says: "The accused is not in possession of several exhibits listed for this municipality. " That's all very well. But he may have sent it in the e-mail to Ms. Gustin, she hasn't had a chance to check it, but if he hasn't, can we know which ones he says he's missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: He has sent an e-mail and numbered every exhibit that was missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it should be easy. Yes, Mr. Brdjanin, have you been handed these two documents? Mrs. Baruch? This one and this one?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the witness before may have been right because I think I did see an insignia of the Wolves of Vucjak with the mouth open. I remember very, very, very vividly having seen one, either in one of the films, or video clips.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That may be in, Your Honour, because in fact, he's stills I think were taken from one of the videos but I don't think there is much dispute about this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. So now, sir, what's going to happen is that you are going to be cross-examined by the Defence team for Mr. Brdjanin. As I explained to you before, the Defence here is doing its duty and you have every responsibility and every duty that -- to answer, and obligation to answer each question that is put to you the same way you have answered the questions put to you by the Prosecution. Yes, Mrs. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Barbara Baruch. I represent the defendant in this case. Mr. Witness, you were aware when you walked into this room that the defendant would be under guard, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assumed something like that but I didn't know it for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the defendant in this case is the only person under guard in this room; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the only person who doesn't appear to have an official position in this room, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't be able to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you some questions, first about your statement, and then about your testimony. If you don't understand my question or if I speak too quickly for you, will you let me know? Yes? Okay. You said that there was a demand to turn in weapons. Who communicated that demand to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To me personally? Nobody, because I didn't have hunting weapons. However, there was a story circulating the village, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So you learned about the demand to turn in weapons through just gossip in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was some kind of an announcement, and then a neighbour would pass it on to his neighbour and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: When you say there was an "announcement," was there a meeting that you heard about but didn't go to at which the announcement was made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So when you were told about turning in weapons, did the person explain where they heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was something that was spontaneously spread around.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: How did you know to -- which place to turn in your weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We knew because it was said that the weapons ought to be turned over in front of the culture centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You said that somebody gave you a weapon. Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What weapon do you have in mind? The hunting one or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] It's the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think this will make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: You said the hunting or something else. Did you also have a hunting gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't have a hunting weapon. What I had in mind was the surrender, because there were two instances where weapons were surrendered, on the first instance it applied only to hunting weapons. And then there was a second instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And on which instance did --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just interrupt? Your Honour, looking at the screen, the question, you said: Somebody gave you the weapon. Who was that person? And there is no answer to that because it then leads --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, but then we are specifically referring -- we could only be specifically referring to the rifle and no other weapon, because that's the only occasion when he said that he had been given the rifle as a present.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I think he gave an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He never mentioned who.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. I thought he did. All right. Then I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was: Who gave you that weapon. Who was it that gave you that weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a friend of mine, while I still worked in Croatia. It was a small-calibre rifle which was used mostly for hunting.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And was that a friend from Lisnja or the Prnjavor area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. He was from Pakrac, Lipik. I spent a lot of time working there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And are those two places in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you pay for those -- that gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Nothing. When people were there as refugees, they used to come and see me, as a friend, because we had known each other for 10 or 15 years, so they would simply stop by to see me. And as they were withdrawing from Croatia, they also occasionally would stop by my house to see me and sometimes we could see each other in Banja Luka as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And on one of these occasions, when somebody stopped by your house, he gave you this rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did any other weapons come through your possession, even if you didn't keep them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know what happened with other people but nothing came to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. That's my question. About to you. Was this rifle the only weapon you ever possessed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the only one I had. I had a permit for a pistol that I never purchased.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Are you saying you got the permit but you never got the pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right. I never bought it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And never in your life did you ever have another weapon but this one rifle? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never. After the war, I got myself a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So what month and year would that have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Because it was so long ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, ten years or more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So after the war, around 1991 or 1992, you got yourself a pistol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I obtained a pistol now, after this war, perhaps it was in 2000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know of other people who had weapons of any sort, firearms, in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There had been stories as to this person had a weapon, that person had a weapon. I can't say whether that is true or not because I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you ever see any other person in Lisnja after 1990 with a weapon? Not a police officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Territorial Defence had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That's the Territorial Defence that was -- consisted of Lisnja residents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Residents of the local commune of Lisnja, the population in Lisnja was mixed. There were Serbs and there were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I thought Lisnja was mostly Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lisnja itself, yes, but the hamlet of Milosavci which was part of the local commune of Lisnja had residents who were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. The TO that would patrol in Lisnja, that was mostly Bosniak members, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. There were Serbs there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you know the percentage of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that with certainty, since I wasn't a member of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So how do you know that there were Serbs there as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I know the people. I used to come across them. They would be there patrolling all day long. The commander was a Serb. And I used to know him from before, when I was a member of the reserve.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So you used to be a member of the reserve yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I believe that about -- there were about 48 members from Lisnja of the TO that patrolled in Lisnja. Do you know anything that disagrees with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the figure. I know that it existed but how large it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So would it also be true that you don't know the number of Serbs in that TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could say that, yes. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say it was mixed, you really have no knowledge of how many Serbs and how many Bosniaks; is that right? Except for the captain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a captain. There were members, yes. But as to the exact strength of it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. In fact, the Bosnian members of the TO were all issued weapons. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware of that. I saw them with weapons, all of them had weapons without any difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And ammunition? You saw them with ammunition as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. Perhaps they had it packed somewhere but I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Are you aware that the people, the Bosnian members of the TO, did not have their TO M48, I believe, rifles, taken back from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't present when weapons were taken away, so I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And you said, I think, that there were two occasions when someone from the village told you that you had to turn in weapons to the Dom Kultura; is that correct? You were there on two occasions when that became known to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first occasion, when they asked for hunting weapons and weapons with permit, I was there. And on the second occasion, I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And it was on the occasion that you weren't present that your wife turned in the rifle that you had; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: When you say you weren't there, do you mean to tell this Chamber that you were already in the arms of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't consider that to be in the arms of the police because I had an informative interview there, and then that took place, when the weapons were being surrendered. All of us were at the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, it was a poor choice of words. When you went to be interviewed by the police, is when the second request occurred and you were not present? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So on the first occasion, when you were aware that guns were required to be turned in, you personally did not turn in your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And your wife turned the weapon in on her own initiative after you were being interrogated by the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was an order to the effect that anybody who had weapons had to surrender them in front of the culture centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And your wife was the person who decided to take your rifle to the culture centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She had to take it since I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you know or did you know of anybody other than yourself who had a weapon of any sort, who failed to turn in the weapon the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that. Patrols would go around checking, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So you don't know anybody else in Lisnja who had a weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally didn't know about that. Later on when we were in prison, we learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Later on, when you were in prison, you learned that many people from Lisnja had not turned in their weapon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't learn anything in particular. We were interrogated and we, being inside, couldn't know what was going on outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must have misunderstood you. You said something about later on, when you were in detention, you learned about other people who had rifles. Did anybody give you that information? Not question you about it but give you the information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when talking between each other we would hear that because all of us were together so we could talk to each other and we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And some people came into the custody of the Sloga factory after you were first in custody there, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Would some of those people tell you that they had retained their weapons even after the second order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think you were some kind of a Muslim representative in or from Lisnja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was never anything like that. I was never involved in the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: As a person of relative wealth and importance in the community, did you speak up at community meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since my work was away from home, I couldn't really participate in it. I couldn't take on any duties that I wasn't able to discharge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, do you know why anybody would describe you as a Muslim representative in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I did not describe myself as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you hear about people who remained hidden in the woods after June 1st of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody was hidden. There was a person who spent some 10 to 15 days in hiding and then came out and surrendered. There were no consequences for him. So I know only of one person who was hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Who was that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think his name was Osman Rahimic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did Mr. Rahimic have other friends -- strike that, Your Honours. I apologise. How did you hear about Mr. Osman Rahimic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when he came, when he came, he surrendered and the police brought him to Sloga. He told us that he had been in hiding, that he was afraid, and once he got and joined us, he said, "Had I known it was like this, I wouldn't have spent my time hiding."

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So at least one person who later came to the Sloga factory told you that he had a weapon and he was hiding in the woods around Lisnja with that weapon; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that Osman was in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That's what I meant, Mr. Witness. I meant you had a conversation with at least one person who did admit to you that he had a weapon and went into the woods and was hiding. And he told you that at Sloga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether he had a weapon. I know that he was in hiding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But he told you he had a weapon, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. He didn't say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So did Mr. Rahimic tell somebody who then told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: How did you hear about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: About what?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: About Mr. Rahimic hiding in the woods with a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He told you he doesn't know about it. It's the first time he's hearing it from you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's repeatedly stated that he is not aware of what you are hinting at.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think if we go to line 13:28:27, which is still on my screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 13 what?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: My screen says 13:28:27, and it said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That doesn't tally with mine so --

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. One minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think -- the gentleman -- the gun thing was never said by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was assuming I understand the American expression assuming facts not in evidence. At no stage did this witness ever say that he had heard that this man was hiding with a gun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I intervened, Ms. Korner, because I was being patient, allowing the question to be put again, repeatedly, in one way or another, but he's denied it, he's told you straight and plain that he's not aware of what you're hinting at. The only thing that he's aware of is that this individual had spent some time hiding in the woods before he was brought to the Sloga factory. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And that when -- let me ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, Mr. Rahimic told you that after he was hiding he turned in his gun and turned himself in; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. That's not what he said to me. We heard that he had been in hiding and that he came and surrendered and then was imprisoned together with us. He never mentioned any weapons. I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Did you hear, when you were -- before you were in Sloga or when you were in Sloga, that two groups of about 10 to 15 men each took weapons that had been turned in to the police or the TO, that captain, at gunpoint? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that there had been some incidents in Lisnja; however, I couldn't give you any details.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Incidents of what, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Involving weapons. However, I wasn't present so I couldn't say anything more.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Excuse me. You heard of incidents involving weapons, and involving some young men who took weapons? Is that what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether they took weapons or not. Perhaps somebody else could speak about that, but I wasn't present so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So you wouldn't know if there was armed resistance in Lisnja while you were at Sloga; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no shooting at all. Lisnja was shelled, though. However, there was no response from Lisnja, at least that's what I heard, since I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did you hear that there were any police or any VRS or any paramilitaries who were killed or injured near Lisnja, or in Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that three or four young men got killed, Bosniaks, that they had been killed. That's what I heard. I don't know whether any police members were injured or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So your response to my question is: You never heard of any police or VRS or paramilitary person who was killed or injured in or near Lisnja? Is that your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that some people were killed but not troops, rather civilians. As to policemen and the regular army, I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, did you -- you said that you saw a truck of people in military uniforms that just drove through Lisnja; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The shooting, if any, that occurred on that occasion -- well, first, did you witness any shooting on that occasion, yourself, personally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were shooting while riding around. Nobody was injured. Nobody was harassed. Nothing came out of it. They were simply shooting and cursing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, that's not the question. The question was a very simple, straightforward one again. Did you personally witness any of the shooting that has been mentioned? Did you see anyone -- did you see these soldiers shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And that shooting was like young soldiers, here I am, I'm brave, I'm strong, shooting in the air, look at me? That kind of shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if that was done by any Muslim soldiers, any Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They weren't there at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: How would you know if somebody is a Bosniak or a Serb just seeing them in a military truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. I meant Lisnja, when I said that, because there were no troops in Lisnja. However, I don't know who the people on the truck were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So you don't know if they were Bosniaks or Serbs or anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say also that they just drove by where you were so you saw them only for a few seconds or a minute perhaps? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a brief period of time. They simply drove past us. The village is quite large. And they drove through the village. And I'm repeating again, nothing came out of it. Nobody was killed or hurt by those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember that you said in your statement, and here in this courtroom, that you had no idea why the police were looking for you? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They asked me to come in for an informative interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But you did know at the time that you had in your possession a rifle of very small calibre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And you also knew at that time that a request had been made generally for all weapons to be turned in? You knew that as well, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no announcement yet at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I thought you told me there were two announcements, once before and once after you were in custody, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One was before, but it only applied to hunting weapons and the ones with permits. And the other instance was after we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I need to understand that clearly. When you said hunting weapons and with permits, you meant your belief was it had to be both a hunting weapon and have a permit before it was required to be turned in? Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether at that time I already had this rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, when was this first announcement made that weapons or when did you first hear that an announcements had been made that you had to turn in weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the date, but in any case, it was in the spring. I don't remember what month it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, did you go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In the spring of 1992, did somebody come and visit you and give you a gift of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. People did come, my acquaintances that is, and some would even sleep at my place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And give you a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Some also left tractors, and other things, all sorts of things they left with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But I'm not interested in the tractors. What I want to know is: Did people in the spring of 1992 come to your house, visit with you, and leave you weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This guy did leave me a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: At your house in the spring of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which month exactly but, yeah, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: So just about the time when the weapons are being collected from everybody, you have a visitor who comes and brings you a weapon. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know when the weapons were collected elsewhere. I know when they were collected in Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: When you were looking at P1800, which is under seal, do you know which document I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't expect the witness to be asked to refer to exhibits by number. We are talking of the document which was shown to you where supposedly you had been tried and sentenced in 1994. That's what we are talking about. Yes, Mrs. Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. You remember that document so that if you were convicted of possession of a firearm or explosive material between March and May of 1992, it would have been true that you actually had that firearm between the months of March and May of 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what months those were but yes there was this rifle but it was handed over in due time and it was supposed to be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And the fact that you admit it was handed over means you admit it had been in your possession between March and May of 1992, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not in my possession. I didn't use it. I didn't have it. It was in my house. It was just left in my house and finally it ended where it was supposed to end.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Was there a weapon possessed or in your house that belonged to your father or another relative as well as this particular rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My father was old. He was a disabled person. He did not have anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: My question wasn't only limited to your father. I said a weapon that belonged to somebody else that was kept in your house. Were you aware of any others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people in my house just occasionally. They would come and go. What they had on them, I wasn't in the position to know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think your statement says that you were at a cousin's house. You said in court today you were at your neighbour's house. Was your neighbour also your cousin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was my cousin, my relative.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And when you were at your cousin's house, did you or he have a weapon with you or with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And how far away was this cousin's house from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe 20 or 30 metres. We are neighbours so our houses were close.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did you actually recognise any of the police as they were walking up to your house or your cousin's house? Or did you just see a tall person who was in a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not sure whether it was Dragan Mehtic but then when I reported to the police, he confirmed that it had been him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did at any time Dragan Mehtic ask you if you had any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I was being interviewed, I was asked whether I had any weapons, and whether the weapons had been handed over. In other words, whether I had any and whether I surrendered them, and then I told them yes, when I learned that it was supposed to be handed over, that's exactly what I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: But you didn't do it. Your wife did it. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I heard that she had done it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you saw Senijad Mujanic and Zinaid Gusic at the police station, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember from the document that the police -- that the Prosecutor showed you that Senijad Mujanic was also later convicted of possession of firearms or explosives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I only saw it now when you -- when this document has been shown to me. Up to that moment, this was all unfamiliar to me. I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you didn't know about the document, but were you familiar with the fact that Senijad Mujanic actually did possess a firearm or explosive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't know anything like that. It was the first time that I saw this plus the conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Now, Zinaid Gusic whom you also saw, you gave him your car keys, I think you said, because you didn't know when you would go back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that I did not say that I did not know when I would be back, but I had heard that there was a state of chaos in Lisnja and I gave him my car to take it from in front of the police station where it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: To take it home because you didn't believe that you yourself would be able to take it home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. I assumed because of the turmoil. I didn't know what to think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So when you first saw the police officer coming, you ran away, and then when you got to the police station, you gave your car keys to somebody else because you didn't believe that you would be able to drive home yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It's not. That was not the sequence. I reported to the police on Saturday. Then they told me to come back on Monday. I came by my car. We had a short conversation. They took me into a room and it was only in the evening or late in the afternoon, or -- when this happened. I did ask them whether I could come by my own car and they said yes, you can, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: That you could go home in your own car? They said you could? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. As soon as I arrived they asked me: How did you get here? I said: By car. And they said: Okay. So everything was okay. There was no hint as to show me that something unusual was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry, again I'm confused. You actually went to the police station two times. The first was on Saturday and they told you, Drago Mehtic wasn't there and you should come back on Monday, right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dragan Mehtic was not there but they called him and he came in civilian clothes. He then told me: Can you come back Monday? I went home and I came back Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. So when you gave your keys to Gusic, was that on Saturday or on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on Monday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And it wasn't only Bosniaks who were being detained? You also saw a person you identified as a Serbian soldier who was being held in police custody while you were there, isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And I am assuming it was at least on Monday, not on Saturday, that you saw these other people who you knew from Lisnja in the jail; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did say that this was on Monday. I did not mention Saturday in that context.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And one of the people that you saw on Monday was that Abdulah Seperovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did you notice on the document that the Prosecutor handed you that Mr. Seperovic was also convicted of possession of a firearm and/or explosives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw a number of names, probably his name was also there, but I did not actually see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we have the witness hold that exhibit so that he won't have to guess?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, usher, please, could you hand Document P1800 to the witness? Could you refer him, Madam Baruch, to page or number?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I think it's Number 38, if I've got it right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, please go to Number 38. And your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: He was a person, that is Abdulah Seperovic was a person who was also convicted of possession of a firearm or explosives, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, judging by this document, this indeed was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And while you were in the jail, you also saw Sead Dzinic, didn't you? Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dzinic is a hamlet. I don't know people from that hamlet that well so I can't be so sure. This is a bit further from my village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. I thought in your statement that you specifically mentioned him, or at least you specifically mentioned the name Dzinic on page 3 of your statement, didn't you see somebody named Dzinic while you were at the jail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were a number of people with that family name. There is a whole family bearing the same name in that hamlet, and the hamlet itself is called the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you if you saw Sead Dzinic at the jail when you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who Sead Dzinic is. Maybe he was. I may have seen him, but I don't know him. I can't put a face to that name. I don't know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And you saw several people in the jail whose name was Halilic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes, there were quite a few people bearing that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Like Zijad, yes? Do you know Zijad Halilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zijad?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Could you look at Number 26 on the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think that Zijad was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: For possession of a firearm or explosive in May of 1992? You don't believe that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are mixing things up now because.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, microphone, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are mixing things up because first you ask I don't think that Zijad was -- he says: I don't think that Zijad was in prison. Well, obviously, what you are referring to is the -- you weren't referring to prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I was referring to the jail at which this witness was in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. So we have to get this clear and before we get this clear, I think what we need to get from the witness is whether he knew that Zijad Halilic, number one; and secondly, whether Zijad Halilic was with him at the time in the Sloga.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: In the jail. In the jail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or in the jail. Sir, did you know Zijad Halilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew -- I do know Zijad Halilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see him in the jail? Which jail?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, does he mean the police station or at the factory or the Dom Kultura?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you see him in any of these three places that Ms. Korner has just mentioned, the police --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: How about Izet Halilic, Number 15? Did you see him in the jail cell at the police station when you were there on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. He wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have to finish here because we have already gone beyond our limit and I don't want to keep -- yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I just want to ask -- I don't know what page of her 19 pages of cross-examination we are on so I know whether or not to bring my witness -- or how much more there is so I don't bring him too early.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I can only say that some of my questions will disappear upon responsive answers. So if you want to know what page number I'm looking at right now, it's page 3 but I have added a lot of questions from direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So 10.00 a.m. should be safe?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I don't know. I would be more than happy to come at whatever time the Court says and proceed. I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have to stop here. I thank the interpreters and the technicians and everyone else for bearing with us. I'm sorry to have gone beyond the limits, the time limits. Thank you. And we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
